result:
Most people think streetlights only make light. If you ask them what a city sounds like at three in the morning, they will tell you about the distant wash of the interstate, the occasional groan of a garbage truck braking two avenues over, or the dry hiss of wind through oak leaves that haven’t quite decided to fall.

If you stand still long enough—truly still, with your heels together and your jaw unclenched—you hear the fourth thing. You hear the hum.

It is a low, amber vibration, somewhere between a refrigerator and a hive of sleeping bees. In the older districts, where the city council hasn’t yet swapped out the high-pressure sodium lamps for cold white LEDs, the lights sing in F-sharp. They are supposed to, anyway. When a ballast begins to age, or when water seeps into the housing after a three-day October rain, the pitch drifts. It flattens out, sliding down toward F-natural, or worse, hovers in the sickly crack between notes.

When a whole block slips out of tune, people wake up with headaches. Dogs bark at empty corners. Couples argue about who forgot to lock the back door, neither of them realizing it is just the corner of Fourth and Sycamore rubbing against their nerves like a wet finger on the rim of a glass.

That’s why the city still pays me, though my title on the payroll is simply *Electrical Maintenance, Grade II*. 

I walk the grid between midnight and four, carrying a canvas bag over my shoulder. Inside there is a crescent wrench, two rolls of friction tape, a pair of insulated gloves, and three steel tuning forks wrapped in chamois cloth. I don’t use a bucket truck unless a pole is completely dead. Mostly, you just have to listen, climb halfway up the aluminum ladder, crack the housing, and adjust the tension screw on the transformer until the dissonance resolves.

Tonight, the air smells like wet wool and crushed acorns. A fog has rolled in off the river, thick enough to turn every streetlamp into a fuzzy apricot suspended in dark water. I start at the rail yard and work my way uphill toward the library.

By two-fifteen, I’ve fixed three lamps. One on Mercer Street was rattling like a loose tooth; a wasp nest the size of a plum had dried out inside the fixture and was vibrating against the glass. I scraped it out, wiped the lens with my sleeve, and stood at the base of the pole until the hum settled back into its warm, steady drone.

At the corner of Pine and Eleventh, though, I stop. 

There is a lamp there, leaning slightly over a mailbox, that isn’t humming at all. It’s lit—pouring a clean cone of yellow onto the slick sidewalk and the rusted fender of a parked Subaru—but it makes no sound. 

I tilt my head back. Water drips from the brim of my cap onto my nose. I pull the F-sharp fork from my bag, strike it sharply against the rubber sole of my boot, and hold the stem against the cold metal of the pole. 

Usually, the pole acts like the body of a cello, catching the vibration and throwing it back into my palm. Tonight, the metal drinks the sound and gives nothing back. Dead quiet.

I set up the ladder. As I climb into the cone of light, the fog feels thicker up here, warm around the bulb. I unlatch the cover and swing it open, expecting a blown capacitor or a wire chewed bare by a squirrel. 

Everything inside is dry. Clean as a whistle. The wiring is neat, braided copper, older than I am, without a speck of corrosion. 

I stand there on the fourth rung, gloved hand resting on the rim of the housing, looking down the empty street. Two blocks away, a traffic light clicks from red to green for nobody. Above me, the silent bulb glows, effortless and calm. Through the fog, I can hear the other lamps further down Pine Street—a faint, distant chorus, holding the neighborhood together like stitches in a coat.

And here, at Pine and Eleventh, there is just a pocket of nothing. Not a broken thing. Just a rest in the measure.

I reach into my pocket, pull out a stub of chalk, and make a small mark on the inside of the housing so the day crew knows I checked it. Then I close the latch, tighten the screw, and climb back down.

Walking away, I don’t look back, though I can feel the quiet following me for half a block—a brief, gentle relief before the city’s hum closes back over my head, keeping time until morning.
